query: For high-entropy alloys used in thermal-insulation applications, what testable hypothesis could be made about an unspecified predictive approach for accurately identifying materials with low phonon thermal conductivity? The hypothesis should explain why the approach would work, predict its improvement over current predictions, define its applicability limits, identify supporting evidence, and specify a decisive experimental benchmark and outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: A multi-fidelity machine learning framework that integrates advanced phonon transport calculations with experimental inelastic scattering data will more accurately identify disordered high-entropy alloys having low phonon thermal conductivity compared to conventional prediction methods that do not account for the full complexity of mass and force-constant fluctuations.
generation.material_initial_state: Disordered high-entropy alloys (HEAs) in a single-phase, chemically random solid solution intended for thermal insulation applications.
generation.intervention: Implementation of a multi-fidelity data-driven/machine learning model that incorporates both state-of-the-art ab initio phonon transport calculations (e.g., Green–Kubo-based evaluations of phonon lifetimes) and experimental inelastic scattering data.
generation.conditions: The framework is applied over a defined range of HEA compositions exhibiting significant compositional disorder and is validated for thermal conductivity measurements at room temperature up to moderately high temperatures relevant for insulation applications.
generation.structural_mediator: Enhanced mass and force-constant fluctuations inherent to chemical disorder, which reduce phonon lifetimes and enable stronger phonon scattering.
generation.mechanism: By quantitatively capturing how compositional complexity in HEAs leads to increased phonon scattering and reduced lattice thermal conductivity, the model predicts thermal transport properties more accurately than conventional methods that inadequately address multi-component scattering effects.
generation.predicted_outcome: The integrated predictive approach is expected to improve the accuracy of lattice thermal conductivity predictions (e.g., by a relative improvement in prediction error, possibly on the order of 15–20% better fit to experimental data) for HEAs exhibiting complex disorder compared to current models.
generation.baseline: Existing prediction methods based solely on empirical or simpler theoretical mappings that do not fully incorporate detailed phonon scattering physics or leverage inelastic scattering data.
generation.boundary: The model’s improved accuracy is anticipated to hold for chemically disordered, single-phase HEAs; it may not generalize to ordered or partially ordered alloys or systems where additional scattering mechanisms dominate beyond mass/force-constant fluctuations.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of improvement (e.g., the % error reduction) is uncertain and may vary across different regions of the HEA compositional space; further experimental benchmarking is required to fully establish the limits of applicability.

falsification_experiment.design: Select a series of HEA compositions predicted by the machine learning framework to have exceptionally low lattice thermal conductivity. Synthesize these alloys and perform temperature-dependent phonon transport measurements using inelastic neutron scattering and direct thermal conductivity measurements (e.g., via the Green–Kubo method). Simultaneously, benchmark results against predictions from conventional models.
measurements: Lattice thermal conductivity over a temperature range (e.g., 300–700 K)
Phonon lifetimes and attenuation as measured by inelastic neutron or X-ray scattering
Comparative data from conventional predictive approaches
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the experimentally measured lattice thermal conductivity and phonon scattering profiles in the screened HEAs do not show a statistically significant improvement in predictive accuracy (e.g., less than the targeted ~15–20% reduction in prediction error) relative to conventional methods, or if the predicted low-conductivity behavior is not observed, then the hypothesis is falsified.

AbstractHigh-Entropy Alloys (HEAs) are a new family of crystalline random alloys with four or more elements in a simple unit cell, at the forefront of materials research for their exceptional mechanical properties. Their strong chemical disorder leads to mass and force-constant fluctuations which are expected to strongly reduce phonon lifetime, responsible for thermal transport, similarly to glasses. Still, the long range order would associate HEAs to crystals with a complex disordered unit cell. These two families of materials, however, exhibit very different phonon dynamics, still leading to similar thermal properties. The question arises on the positioning of HEAs in this context. Here we present an exhaustive experimental investigation of the lattice dynamics in a HEA, Fe20Co20Cr20Mn20Ni20, using inelastic neutron and X-ray scattering. Typically, the thermal conductivity of these compounds lies below 1 W/(m K). The reasons, or the conjunction of reasons, for this low thermal conductivity have been identified by means of the combined density-functional theory and Boltzmann transport theory approaches. The investigations have evidenced large Grüneisen parameters, low-lying optical and acoustic phonon frequencies, short phonon lifetime, and the presence of defects. cited_evidence.text: Using the same approach, the value of κL was computed for various temperatures in the range 300–700 K (Figure 9). At 300 K, the κL value is 0.4 W K−1 m−1, which is a very low value of the lattice thermal conductivity, favorable for thermoelectric materials. This is due to the lattice distortion effect of high-entropy alloys that can reduce phonon velocity and enhance phonon scattering, resulting in low thermal conductivity. Additionally, one can observe that when the temperature rises, the thermal conductivity of the lattice decreases, which is also due to an increase in phonon scattering at higher temperatures.

decision.trend: Early data-driven approaches demonstrated how machine learning could efficiently screen high-entropy alloy (HEA) compositions for certain properties, yet these methods primarily emphasized mechanical attributes. More recent research on phonon behavior in disordered HEAs has revealed significant phonon scattering effects that reduce lattice thermal conductivity and complicate its prediction. Despite progress in modeling scattering from first principles, there is no widely validated, high-throughput computational or data-driven framework dedicated to identifying low-thermal-conductivity HEAs specifically for thermal-insulation applications.
decision.unsolved: Existing predictions do not fully quantify or validate how compositional complexity, mass disorder, and force-constant fluctuations collectively suppress phonon conduction in HEAs. While data-driven screening is maturing, robust models that accurately capture the multicomponent phonon scattering physics and systematically validate predictions across the entire composition space remain lacking.
decision.lever: Develop a multi-fidelity machine-learning framework that integrates advanced phonon transport calculations (e.g., Green-Kubo or ab initio methods) and experimental inelastic scattering data to systematically identify and validate low thermal conductivity in disordered HEAs. Model parameters will incorporate mass/force-constant fluctuations, compositional complexity, and phonon lifetime measurements.
decision.why: This approach combines the large-scale composition screening of data analytics with precise phonon scattering models, directly addressing the core challenge of predicting and experimentally verifying phonon transport in highly disordered HEAs. It leverages newly available lattice dynamics data, bridging theoretical insights and informatics-driven exploration to refine and validate thermal-insulation materials discovery.
